claim: The stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab, Cancer borealis, contains the neurons that generate two stomach rhythms, the fast pyloric rhythm and the slower gastric mill rhythm.
source: The stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab, Cancer borealis, contains the neurons that generate two stomach rhythms, the fast pyloric rhythm and the slower gastric mill rhythm.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the STG structure and function.

claim: The pyloric rhythm is driven by a three-neuron pacemaker kernel consisting of one Anterior Burster (AB) and two Pyloric Dilator (PD) neurons.
source: The pyloric rhythm is driven by a three-neuron pacemaker kernel – one Anterior Burster (AB) and two Pyloric Dilator (PD) neurons.
evidence: This describes the known cellular composition of the pyloric pacemaker.

claim: The Lateral Pyloric (LP) and Pyloric (PY) neurons fire out of phase with the PD neurons because they are rhythmically inhibited by the PD/AB group.
source: The Lateral Pyloric (LP) and Pyloric (PY) neurons fire out of phase with the PD neurons because they are rhythmically inhibited by the PD/AB group (Marder and Bucher, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cardiac ganglion (CG) generates the rhythm responsible for heart contraction.
source: The cardiac ganglion (CG) generates the rhythm responsible for heart contraction, and consists of four pacemaker Small Cell (SC) neurons that drive five motor Large Cell (LC) neurons (Cooke, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cardiac ganglion consists of four pacemaker Small Cell (SC) neurons that drive five motor Large Cell (LC) neurons.
source: The cardiac ganglion (CG) generates the rhythm responsible for heart contraction, and consists of four pacemaker Small Cell (SC) neurons that drive five motor Large Cell (LC) neurons (Cooke, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Increasing pH reveals non-linear effects on activity, which may suggest more complex mechanisms.

claim: The physiological properties of ion channels are sensitive to pH.
source: Given that the physiological properties of ion channels are sensitive to pH (Anwar et al., 2017; Bayliss et al., 2015; Catterall, 2000; Cens et al., 2011; Cook et al., 1984; Doering and McRory, 2007; Guarina et al., 2017; Harms et al., 2017; Hille, 1968; Mahapatra et al., 2011; Marcantoni et al., 2010; Tombaugh and Somjen, 1996; Vilin et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2018), one might imagine that a neuronal circuit might be as sensitive to changes in pH as its most sensitive ion channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is surprising that the central pattern generating rhythms of both the STG and the CG of the crab, C. borealis, are relatively insensitive to acute pH change from about pH 6.1 to pH 8.8.
source: Therefore, it is surprising that the central pattern generating rhythms of both the STG and the CG of the crab, C. borealis, are relatively insensitive to acute pH change from about pH 6.1 to pH 8.8 while the individual functions of many ion channels are known to be considerably altered within this range.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data in the current study compared to known ion channel properties.

claim: The individual functions of many ion channels are known to be considerably altered within the pH range from 6.1 to 8.8.
source: Therefore, it is surprising that the central pattern generating rhythms of both the STG and the CG of the crab, C. borealis, are relatively insensitive to acute pH change from about pH 6.1 to pH 8.8 while the individual functions of many ion channels are known to be considerably altered within this range.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on ion channels.

claim: One possible explanation for these results is that crustacean ion channels are more robust to pH change than channels from other species.

claim: In most vertebrate animals, pH is carefully regulated.
source: In most vertebrate animals, pH is carefully regulated.

claim: Slight acidosis or alkalosis can have deleterious effects on many aspects of vertebrate physiology.
source: Slight acidosis or alkalosis can have deleterious effects on many aspects of vertebrate physiology (Chesler, 2003; Fencl et al., 1966; Nattie, 1999), which may be partially a consequence of the relative sensitivity of many vertebrate ion channels and synapses to pH.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Little is known about the pH sensitivity of crustacean ion channels.
source: Unfortunately, little is known about the pH sensitivity of crustacean ion channels, but it would be surprising if it differed drastically from that seen in other animals as there is considerable homology across phylogeny in channel structure and function.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: It would be surprising if crustacean ion channel pH sensitivity differed drastically from that seen in other animals as there is considerable homology across phylogeny in channel structure and function.
source: Unfortunately, little is known about the pH sensitivity of crustacean ion channels, but it would be surprising if it differed drastically from that seen in other animals as there is considerable homology across phylogeny in channel structure and function.
evidence: This is an inference based on known evolutionary conservation of ion channels.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that acid-sensing ion channels are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Recent evidence suggests that acid-sensing ion channels are evolutionarily conserved, which presents the possibility of specialized channels for the modulation of pH in crustacean ganglia (Lynagh et al., 2018).

source: Another possibility for the circuit robustness seen in this study could be that there are compensatory and/or correlated changes in the effects of pH across the population of channels in these networks.
